title: Dependency approval and intake
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: Every direct dependency is on an approved register with purpose, owner, license, maintainer health and risk rating; new or changed dependencies, including new transitive packages, fail the build until an intake decision is recorded; preference is given to fewer, well-maintained dependencies and to the .NET base library over third-party packages.
current_practice: SEC-SUPPLY-001 is a proposed rule. No dependency register or intake gate was located. Limen describes its browser library as dependency-free.
intended_practice: Every direct dependency is on an approved register with purpose, owner, license, maintainer health and risk rating; new or changed dependencies, including new transitive packages, fail the build until an intake decision is recorded; preference is given to fewer, well-maintained dependencies and to the .NET base library over third-party packages.
provable: Nothing for a production service; no Echelon production system exists as of 2026-11-25.
customer_statement: Echelon intends to implement this as part of Unbound's initial build; it is not in operation today and no evidence is available yet.

title: Lockfiles, pinning and reproducible restore
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: NuGet restores in locked mode from committed packages.lock.json, npm uses npm ci with a committed package-lock.json, CI actions are pinned to full commit SHAs, container images to digests, and the build fails on any unpinned reference.

title: Build integrity and SLSA provenance
status_rationale: Release workflows for Echelon's published tools (Praxis, Limen, Strata) are configured to generate GitHub build-provenance attestations; there is no product build, and SLSA level has not been assessed.
target_answer: Release artifacts are built only by a hosted, ephemeral build service from version-controlled workflow definitions, never from developer machines; each artifact carries signed SLSA provenance recording repository, commit, workflow and builder; Echelon targets SLSA Build Level 3 for production artifacts and states its achieved level with evidence.
current_practice: Praxis, Limen and Strata release workflows include actions/attest-build-provenance; Limen's publish workflow verifies attestations with gh attestation verify before publishing. Workflow runs and achieved SLSA level were not verified. No Unbound build exists.
intended_practice: Release artifacts are built only by a hosted, ephemeral build service from version-controlled workflow definitions, never from developer machines; each artifact carries signed SLSA provenance recording repository, commit, workflow and builder; Echelon targets SLSA Build Level 3 for production artifacts and states its achieved level with evidence.
provable: Workflow definitions in tool repositories (praxis@12bf9951, limen@743cdb9b, strata@c6a384ec); published attestations, if any, can be checked publicly but were not checked here.
customer_statement: Echelon's published developer tools are released through hosted build workflows configured to produce signed build-provenance attestations. Production service builds do not exist yet; SLSA-aligned provenance is planned for them.

challenge.customer_intent: Know that what runs is what was reviewed.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Build system compromise inserts malicious code, as in known build-server attacks.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional questionnaires ask about change control and code review, which do not detect build-time tampering.
challenge.legally_required: No; OMB M-22-18 attestation for federal software references provenance practices.
challenge.contractually_required: Rarely today; growing in federal and large enterprise procurement.
challenge.historical_convention: Internal build servers with administrator access.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Hosted ephemeral builders and signed provenance remove developer-machine builds and make tampering detectable when consumers verify.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Release workflows emit attestations; deployment verifies them.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Provenance by construction plus verification at deploy.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely positive; many customers will not yet know how to use it.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Builds outside the hosted workflow; actions pinned by mutable tags; repository administrators able to alter workflows without review.
challenge.alternative_risks: Hosted build provider becomes a trusted party; provenance proves origin, not absence of malicious source.
supporting_arguments: Already partly configured in tool repositories.
opposing_arguments: Mixed action pinning undermines the integrity of the build definition.
Provenance without deploy-time verification has little effect.

challenge.customer_intent: Avoid depending on abandoned or poorly secured open-source projects.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Questionnaires ask whether open source is assessed; answers are usually narrative.
challenge.historical_convention: Ad hoc developer judgment and SCA vulnerability alerts.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not applicable; fewer dependencies reduces exposure.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Minimize dependencies, measure the rest, publish own Scorecard.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Treating a high score as proof of safety; Scorecard cannot detect a malicious maintainer.
challenge.alternative_risks: Gaming or misreading scores; heuristic checks with false positives for small, stable projects.
opposing_arguments: Scores are proxies; a well-scored project can still be compromised.
Small stable libraries may score poorly while being low risk.
